summary: This Engadget excerpt from Holly Jean Buck's essay in Democracy in a Hotter Time (ed. David W. Orr, MIT Press, 2023) argues that climate change, rising authoritarianism and internet platform dominance are interacting to worsen one another. Buck contends that the current attention-monetizing internet, with algorithms optimized for anger, is a central obstacle to climate action and the energy transition. She frames the internet as a global emotional 'endocrine system' rather than a rational network and says even the climate movement's idea of energy democracy needs rethinking.
one_line: Holly Jean Buck argues the outrage-driven, platform-dominated internet, alongside rising authoritarianism, blocks the political consensus and infrastructure needed for climate action.
key_facts: Democracy in a Hotter Time: Climate Change and Democratic Transformation is edited by David W. Orr and published by MIT Press in 2023.
Holly Jean Buck is Assistant Professor of Environment and Sustainability at the University at Buffalo and a contributing author.
About four billion people, or 54 percent of the world, in ninety-five countries live under fully authoritarian or competitive authoritarian regimes.
Buck says Russia's most recent invasion of Ukraine stripped away any illusion that globalization succeeded or that the twenty-first century broke from the brutal twentieth.
Buck's thesis is that the current configuration of the Internet is a key obstacle to climate action.
Algorithms that profit from maximizing time-on-site have learned that anger keeps people clicking; David Courtwright calls the addictive system 'limbic capitalism'.
Evgeny Morozov quipped, 'Post-truth is to digital capitalism what pollution is to fossil capitalism — a by-product of operations.'
Buck says framing the problem as 'misinformation' or 'disinformation' treats it as bad content poisoning the well rather than a rotten structure.
Geert Lovink recalled a 1996 interview in which John Perry Barlow described cyberspace connecting every synapse of all citizens on the planet.
Buck describes the internet as a collective brain acting like an emotional toddler, more like a global endocrine system than a computer.
Authoritarians run troll farms that can manipulate the range of solutions and sentiments about them.

Buck lists mechanisms of obstruction: false climate information, political polarization, infighting within the climate movement, networked opposition to energy infrastructure, constant distraction, and time drained from real-world action.
The essay focuses on how media ecology interferes with climate strategy and infrastructure, and on energy democracy: renewable, small-scale systems and community control.
